opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I'd do is spend a lot of it on something that sounds unglamorous: just watching children, carefully and at scale, in the places where they actually live and learn. Most of what we know about early learning comes from a pretty narrow slice of kids, often the children of university professors in places like Berkeley or Cambridge, tested for ten minutes in a lab. That's been incredibly productive, but it's a strange sample. So I'd want a big chunk of the money to go to long-term, cross-cultural studies, following children in many different communities from infancy through, say, age seven, and recording what they actually do all day: how they play, who they learn from, what they explore.

The second thing is that I'd really focus on play and exploration, which I think are the most important and least understood things children do. We have a lot of evidence that even very young children are doing something like science. They're forming hypotheses, running little experiments, and figuring out causal structure in the world. But we don't really understand how that works in the wild, as opposed to in our carefully controlled experiments. Pretend play in particular is fascinating, because it seems to be connected to counterfactual reasoning, the ability to think about how things could be different. I'd love to know much more about that.

The third piece, and this is one where we're in a new place now, is to bring together developmental psychology and AI. Children are still the best learners in the known universe. They learn from tiny amounts of data, they generalize brilliantly, and they're intrinsically motivated to explore, in a way our machines still really aren't. So I'd fund collaborations where we put children and AI systems in the same environments, the same little virtual worlds or physical tasks, and compare what they do. That tells us something about the children, and it might also tell us how to build systems that learn more the way children do.

And finally, and this is the part people sometimes find surprising, I'd spend money studying the caregivers, not just the children. Human childhood is so long, and it's paired with this enormous investment of care, from parents, but also from grandparents, siblings, and alloparents of all kinds. I think that's not incidental; it's the whole point. The long, protected childhood is what gives children the freedom to explore. So understanding how care works, and what happens when it's supported or not supported, seems to me just as important as understanding the child's brain. Frankly, if a little of that hundred million ended up going toward actually supporting caregivers, I wouldn't mind that either.

r001.rationale: The response proposes large-scale, long-term studies but does not say that research on young children’s learning can be very inexpensive.

r002.rationale: It proposes observing and recording children’s activities, but does not propose video recorded from babies’ own perspective.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that a hundred million dollars is actually not very much money compared to what we spend on, say, a single particle accelerator or a telescope. And in some ways the problem we're trying to solve, how a two-year-old manages to learn as much about the world as they do, is at least as hard as anything in physics. So I'd want to spend it on something ambitious rather than just funding more of the same little studies.

What I'd really like to do is build what I sometimes think of as a developmental observatory. Right now most of what we know about children's learning comes from bringing a kid into a lab for twenty minutes, showing them a puppet or a box with a toy inside, and seeing what they do. Those studies have been enormously revealing, but they're snapshots. What we don't have is a rich, continuous picture of what children are actually experiencing and doing over months and years. So I'd want longitudinal, dense recordings of children's everyday lives, what they see, what they hear, what they touch, how caregivers respond to them, across many different cultures, not just middle-class families near research universities. We now have the computational tools to make sense of that kind of data in ways we couldn't even ten years ago.

The second piece, and this is where my current obsessions come in, would be to put that data in direct conversation with artificial intelligence. One of the striking things about the large language models is that they're trained on something like a trillion words, and a child hears maybe thirty million by age three. Yet the child ends up with a kind of understanding of causality, of other minds, of how to intervene in the world, that the systems still don't have. So I'd fund people to build systems that learn the way children do, with curiosity, with exploration, by actually acting on things rather than passively absorbing text, and then test whether those systems can match what we see in the real children. The AI becomes a way of testing our theories, and the children become a benchmark for the AI.

And then the third thing, which people tend to forget, is that children don't learn alone. They learn from caregivers, from grandparents, from older siblings, and the whole arrangement of human childhood, that long helpless period where other people take care of you, is itself the thing that makes the learning possible. So I'd want a good chunk of the money going to studying care itself, what it is that caregivers do, and how we might support it. If I'm honest, I'd probably spend more of the hundred million on that than on anything else, because that's where the real leverage is.

r001.rationale: The response calls $100 million modest compared with major scientific facilities and refers to existing studies as small, but it does not say research on how young children learn can be very inexpensive.

r002.rationale: It proposes dense recordings of children's everyday experiences, but does not specify video recordings or capture from babies' own perspective.

astra-6.text:
I’d use a large part of it to do something that sounds rather simple: find out what children’s everyday lives actually look like. We have these very precise experiments where a child comes into a laboratory, sees a few things, and makes a choice. But we know much less about the experience that leads up to that moment. What do children see? What do they explore? Who talks to them, and how do those people respond?

I’d want to follow children over time, in a wide range of cultures and circumstances, and observe their learning in detail. One of the problems with studying children is that we tend to study the children who happen to live near universities and whose parents have time to bring them into a lab. That’s a very particular sample of human childhood.

Then I’d connect those observations to experiments and computational models. If we think exploration or play is doing something important, can we explain exactly what children learn through it? Can we build a model that learns in a similar way, and use it to make predictions we can test?

The exciting thing would be to connect those levels: the actual richness of a child’s life, the careful experimental question, and a theory of how learning works.

r001.rationale: The response calls for a large research budget and detailed study, but does not say that research on young children’s learning can be very inexpensive.

r002.rationale: It proposes observing children over time, but does not propose video recorded from babies’ own perspective.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d want to study children learning in the places where they actually spend their lives. We’ve learned a tremendous amount from bringing a child into a laboratory for twenty minutes and giving them a very carefully designed problem. But that leaves out most of what makes children such remarkable learners: they’re exploring, playing, asking questions, and interacting with people who care about them.

So I’d use a substantial part of the money to follow children over time, across a much wider range of cultures and circumstances, and get a much richer picture of what they experience. What do they choose to investigate? When do they ask someone else? What happens when an adult helps, and what happens when the adult steps back? You’d want to connect those observations to experiments that could distinguish different explanations of how learning works.

And I’d bring together people who study children with people who build computational models of learning. The interesting question isn’t simply how much information a child absorbs. It’s how a child comes up with a possibility that nobody has explicitly taught them, and then figures out whether it’s true. A hundred million dollars could give us a much better account of that process—and of the environments that allow it to flourish.

r001.rationale: The response discusses allocating a substantial budget to longitudinal observations and experiments, but does not say that research on young children’s learning can be very inexpensive.

r002.rationale: The response proposes observing children in everyday settings, but does not mention studying babies’ experiences through video from their own perspective.
